en: Declaring his authority as guardian,
He pulled him back toward home.
Seytek, growing angry and impassioned, said:
“Ah, my uncle Akjoltoy,
A brave man may indeed be reckless;
When young and drinking liquor,
His mind is thin and he is drunk.
But does a man turn back from death?
Can anyone retreat from his appointed doom?
A valiant man, a heroic man,
Without contending for land or tending a people—
Let such a living soul sink into the earth,
For does not every soul die in the end?
Feeding in hollows and passing his days,
Even the most cowardly creature
Still lives out its allotted time,
But its days pass in fear,
And even a sheep dies among the reeds.
For honor and for dignity,
Does not a heroic youth die?”
So spoke brave Seytek,
Arguing grandly before calming down.
Having gained knowledge through the prize,
He obeyed Akjoltoy,
For Akjoltoy was his appointed guardian;
They separated out and took the horses,
Then turned back and took the road,
Coming at last to camp in Talas.
Riding colts and flying hunting birds,
They ranged the hillsides and hunted deer,
Lived at ease without disquiet,
Played bagalak and raised the dust,
And made broad Talas their summer pasture.
He broke the raiders’ strength,
And set his kinsmen’s hearts at rest;
He kept Talas and made it his land,
A lion of surpassing fortune,
And there he remained.
Let us leave that matter there
And begin the news from elsewhere:
At the edge of Great Beijing,
In a wondrous planted garden,
Upon the throne of great Kite—
Kite’s throne was like this:
A tower raised for pleasure.
Ask not of that tower—
A grove of plane trees surrounded it,
And at its center stood a golden throne.
Before the golden throne,
Upon a mound adorned with jewels,
On a platform built for repose,
Stood a white pavilion with jeweled pillars;
There great Kite lay.
His blue-steel weapon hung at his side,
And a blue-collared robe covered him.
His outstretched legs would not draw in,
His closed eyes would not open;
For many days and many nights
His snoring never ceased.
Unwearyingly he occupied the throne,
Doing entirely as he pleased.
When the pale dawn broke,
And wind moved through the valley,
When stars scattered from the sky
And the earth opened in glimmering light,
As though some man would come bearing news,
Then Kite’s
Snoring subsided,
His eyes opened from sleep,
His outstretched legs drew in,
And his heart heaved in turmoil.
He put on his battle gear,
Set his battle-axe in readiness,
And prepared himself for the hearth of war:
“What has happened to the black ridge
Stretching straight across the pass?
What has happened upon the heights where they camped,
What has happened to the people?”
He was the master of the land and nation,
The giant champion of Beijing,
The khan of its tribal people,
The mainstay within their nest.
The moon had waned and the year rolled on;
“Oh, my child, how many days have passed since then!
The might of one champion
Was equal to that of countless warriors.
He was khan of the forty tribes,
Foremost among the spearmen,
A lion among marksmen.
Great Bilgich and I
Were like ravens croaking as they seize their feast;
Among the forty tribes of this Chinese nation,
He was the son of my own kin…”
Saying this, he stopped;
Look at that infernal man—
He was lamenting great Bilgich.
At that very moment great Bilgich
Entered through the gate.
His Kerik horse wore mourning,
And poor Bilgich was wounded.
His face was pale and haggard;
Good heavens, his figure and bearing,
His form made for the saddle,
His heroic stature and presence—
Far worse than before,
Bilgich’s appearance was utterly ruined.
His color gone, he reeled in confusion,
His power spent and body wasted,
All his strength exhausted.
His mustache bristled hair by hair,
His beard stuck out strand by strand.
His eyes had sunk into their sockets;
His parched lips never closed,
And thick spittle gathered there.
With a life scarcely alive,
With only such strength as kept him from expiring,
His vigor exhausted and power gone—
When they looked upon brave Bilgich,
Black blood had drained from his body.
At times he could regain his speech,
At times he could not speak;
At times his eyes could see,
At times they could not.
His lower lip sagged open—
Great indeed was the torment he had suffered;
His upper lip was drawn away,
And he had returned halfway among the dead.
His fine mustache drooped,
His dim eyes bulged;
He groaned and coughed,
Like one about to depart for the other world.
Great Bilgich, grievously afflicted,
Beat his lungs with every breath.
Beijing’s mightiest boar,
His spirit narrowed and burning with pain,
Thus had great Bilgich arrived;
No soul could endure his groaning—
Such was the state of great Bilgich.
When Bilgich appeared like this,
They had the great doors shut,
And slaughtered eighty black bulls
As sacrificial offerings.
Red-gowned and slender-waisted,
Beautiful women with dainty feet—
For women’s hands were said to bring relief—
Were set to tend him.
They shouted for the skilled healers
And summoned all the physicians.
The physicians of China,
Those who diagnosed by feeling the pulse,
The most accomplished masters of medicine,
Their experts standing forty rows deep—
Now the great physicians examined him.
“Alas, this Burut foe is formidable!
How many men among us
Have been ruined by him?” they said.
The great lungs that drew his breath
“It turned out badly,” he said,
The physician was skillful,
From his wound, with a great probe,
They sucked it all out together.
In the populous realm of China
There are medicines for every need,
Every kind of remedy is there.
They gave him powdered red medicine
To take internally.
The pain of the wound subsided,
His closed eyes opened,
Chongbilgich returned to the light.
When seven days had passed,
Chongbilgich regained his speech,
And slowly began to speak with force,
Addressing his sovereign Kite,
He began these words:
“We were a hundred champions skilled in sorcery,
We broke through their defenses and opened a path,
We attacked that aroused nation.
We saw might surpassing all the world,
We saw great torments like those of hell.
We gathered up the riches,
But all ninety-nine companions
Were slaughtered in a yawning pit.
Chongbilgich alone remained,
I despaired of my precious life;
My prowess did not save me from death,
Never have I seen calamity like this.
I have no commander, no people,
No champion remains to shelter me.
The two giants Akjoltoy and Seytek
Caught me between them,
Yet I escaped their swift steeds,
And turned back after assailing the Buruts.
I went there boasting of valor,
But was parted from my champions,
My ribs and back were battered,
My poor head was split,
Most died beneath the ordeal,
Drenched entirely in blood.
With life scarcely remaining,
With strength enough only to gasp,
I escaped and came back to the khagan.
Would any man dare face them?
From the merciless Kyrgyz host,
Could any man escape alive?
That is what I say—understand it well;
My noble Kite, heed my words.
Many cares lie in my heart:
For the gray-maned hero born of your loins,
What woman could give birth
To a son named Chyngteñir?
I traced the lore of old,
And questioned those who know.
There in the land of India-China,
They say there is a woman worthy of you.
The great Kergi, as he is called,
Is the khan of that India.
In that Indian khan’s house,
I hear there is one worthy of you,
Burul, with her flowing, curling hair,
A daughter surpassing all others.
If you take her, she will bear a lion,
That woman will bear a hero;
No man will have the strength to overcome him,
Not a living soul will pass beyond him.
When that woman bears a son,
The earth will heave and waters overflow,
Cliffs will shift and rocks will fall,
Every living creature will truly writhe.
In fury he will clutch blood in his hands,
He will roar in dreadful majesty,
His lion nature will be revealed;
At his birth a standard will be raised.
When he reaches fifteen years,
He will bring turmoil upon the Buruts;
Countless beasts will be slaughtered for his feast,
And he will be named Teñir.
Chyngteñir himself will be born to you,
When Chyngteñir is born—
When he dons his broad coat,
When he takes the reins and mounts a horse,
Whoever provokes his anger
Chyngteñir will slaughter.
Ninety warriors will be his companions;
When your Kyrgyz rise surging against him,
They will be leveled with the black earth.”
“What you have said is fitting,”
“Your counsel is wise,”
Said great Kite when he heard this,
And throughout every land
Known to ear and seen by eye, he sent word.
To the many tribes of the Chinese nation,
He sent word among the people.
“May God spare us the sight!
The khan’s decree has come,” they said.
Dust rose and haze spread,
As orders drove the people onward;
